Hadean.earth: A molten, then slowly cooling world battered by impacts. A Mars-sized body (Theia) struck the proto-Earth early on, forming the Moon. By ~4.4 Ga a thin crust and the first oceans had formed under a thick CO₂/steam atmosphere with no free oxygen.

Archean.earth: Hotter mantle, small protocontinents and island arcs in a global ocean. The atmosphere was rich in CO₂ and methane and essentially oxygen-free; the young Sun was ~25% fainter. Oceans were green-tinted with dissolved iron, laying down banded iron formations.

Proterozoic.earth: Continents grew and assembled into supercontinents (Columbia, Rodinia, Pannotia). Oxygen rose in the Great Oxidation Event, and the planet froze over in several 'Snowball Earth' glaciations.

Phanerozoic.earth: The eon of 'visible life': continents drifted from scattered pieces into Pangaea and apart again, while life colonised the land, the air and every ocean.

Eoarchean.earth: Scattered crustal fragments in a global ocean; the Late Heavy Bombardment waned. Oldest preserved rocks (Acasta Gneiss, Isua belt).

Paleoarchean.earth: First cratons (Kaapvaal, Pilbara) formed; shallow seas hosted microbial mats. No oxygen in the air.

Mesoarchean.earth: Possible first supercontinent, Vaalbara, and first known glaciation (Pongola). Microbial mats and stromatolites widespread.

Neoarchean.earth: Continental crust grew rapidly; oxygenic photosynthesis became established, setting the stage for the Great Oxidation Event.

Paleoproterozoic.earth: The Great Oxidation Event made the atmosphere oxygenated for the first time; the Huronian glaciation followed. The supercontinent Columbia (Nuna) assembled.

Mesoproterozoic.earth: The 'Boring Billion': stable climate, low oxygen, sulfidic deep oceans. Columbia broke up and Rodinia assembled.

Neoproterozoic.earth: Rodinia broke apart; Earth endured global 'Snowball Earth' glaciations, then oxygen rose again and the first animals appeared.

Paleozoic.earth: Began with scattered continents and warm shallow seas and ended with the assembly of Pangaea. Plants and animals colonised land; vast coal forests grew.

Mesozoic.earth: Pangaea split into Laurasia and Gondwana and then into today's continents; the Atlantic opened. Mostly a warm greenhouse world with no polar ice caps.

Cenozoic.earth: The 'Age of Mammals'. Continents moved to their current positions, India collided with Asia raising the Himalaya, and Earth cooled from a hothouse into the ice ages.

Siderian.earth: Banded iron formations peaked as oxygen from cyanobacteria reacted with iron in the oceans; the Great Oxidation Event began.

Rhyacian.earth: The Huronian glaciation, one of the longest ice ages, gripped the planet. The Bushveld Complex formed.

Orosirian.earth: Intense mountain building (orogenies) on nearly every continent; two huge asteroid impacts (Vredefort, Sudbury).

Statherian.earth: The supercontinent Columbia (Nuna) completed assembly. Oxygen levels stabilised at low levels.

Calymmian.earth: Platform covers expanded over continents as Columbia began to break up.

Ectasian.earth: Continued expansion of platform covers; ocean deep water still low in oxygen.

Stenian.earth: The supercontinent Rodinia assembled through the Grenville orogeny.

Tonian.earth: Rodinia began to rift apart. Oxygen rose and eukaryotic algae diversified.

Cryogenian.earth: 'Snowball Earth': the Sturtian and Marinoan glaciations may have covered the planet in ice nearly to the equator.

Ediacaran.earth: Continents of the former Rodinia drifted apart (Pannotia). Oceans became oxygenated after the Snowball glaciations melted.

Cambrian.earth: Warm greenhouse world with high sea levels flooding the continents; Gondwana lay across the south pole. The land was bare rock and microbial crusts.
Cambrian.sea: Rising steadily from 4 m to 90 m

Ordovician.earth: Continents were scattered with Gondwana in the southern hemisphere; high sea levels and a warm climate until a sharp glaciation at the end triggered a mass extinction.
Ordovician.sea: 180 m; rising to 220 m in Caradoc and falling sharply to 141 m in end-Ordovician glaciations

Silurian.earth: Warm, stable climate after the Ordovician ice age melted. Laurentia and Baltica collided (Caledonian orogeny). Plants began to green the shorelines.
Silurian.sea: Around 180 m, with short-term negative excursions

Devonian.earth: The 'Age of Fishes'. Euramerica ('Old Red Sandstone continent') and Gondwana converged. The first forests spread and soils formed; sea levels high and climate warm.
Devonian.sea: Relatively steady around 189 m, gradually falling to 120 m through period

Carboniferous.earth: Vast swampy coal forests covered the tropics; oxygen peaked at ~35%. Pangaea was assembling and a major ice age gripped Gondwana in the south.
Carboniferous.sea: Falling from 120 m to present-day level throughout the Mississippian, then rising steadily to about 80 m at end of perio

Permian.earth: Pangaea fully assembled, surrounded by the Panthalassa ocean; interiors were vast deserts. Ended with the Siberian Traps eruptions and the largest mass extinction in history.

Triassic.earth: Pangaea at its largest: hot, dry and monsoonal with no polar ice. Life slowly recovered from the Great Dying; the period ended with another mass extinction as Pangaea began to rift.

Jurassic.earth: Pangaea split into Laurasia and Gondwana; the central Atlantic opened. Warm, humid greenhouse climate with lush forests of conifers, cycads and ferns.

Cretaceous.earth: Continents moved toward their modern positions; very high sea levels created inland seaways such as the Western Interior Seaway. Hot greenhouse climate; the period ended with an asteroid impact at Chicxulub.

Paleogene.earth: After the K–Pg extinction, mammals radiated into empty niches. A hot early Eocene (PETM) gave way to cooling and the first Antarctic ice sheets at the Eocene–Oligocene boundary.

Neogene.earth: Continents near modern positions; the Isthmus of Panama closed, Himalaya and Alps rose. Climate cooled and dried and grasslands spread across the continents.

Quaternary.earth: The ice ages: repeated glacial and interglacial cycles, with ice sheets covering North America and northern Eurasia at glacial peaks and sea levels up to 120 m lower.

Terreneuvian.earth: Shallow shelf seas flooded; small shelly fossils appear in abundance as mineralised skeletons evolved.

Cambrian Series 2.earth: Peak of the Cambrian explosion. Famous fossil sites like Chengjiang in China preserve soft-bodied animals.

Miaolingian.earth: Warm oceans; Burgess Shale fauna lived on the edge of Laurentia.

Furongian.earth: A time of repeated trilobite extinctions ('biomere' events) and low diversity called the Furongian gap.

Early Ordovician.earth: High sea levels; the Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event begins.

Middle Ordovician.earth: Peak of the Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event; reefs of bryozoans and corals.
Middle Ordovician.sea: 180 m; rising to 220 m in Caradoc and falling sharply to 141 m in end-Ordovician glaciations

Late Ordovician.earth: Gondwana drifted over the south pole; a brief glaciation ended the Ordovician with the second largest mass extinction.

Llandovery.earth: Recovery after the end-Ordovician extinction; sea levels rose as ice melted.

Wenlock.earth: Warm reefs of tabulate and rugose corals; plants established on land.

Ludlow.earth: Shallow seas; eurypterids reached giant sizes.

Pridoli.earth: Shortest Paleozoic epoch; first jawed fish diversify.

Early Devonian.earth: Land plants spread inland; Rhynie chert preserves an early land ecosystem.

Middle Devonian.earth: First forests of tree-sized plants such as Wattieza.

Late Devonian.earth: Archaeopteris forests; the Late Devonian extinction devastated reefs.
Late Devonian.sea: Relatively steady around 189 m, gradually falling to 120 m through period

Middle Pennsylvanian.earth: Coal forest peak; oxygen very high; giant insects.

Late Pennsylvanian.earth: Carboniferous rainforest collapse as climate dried.

Guadalupian.earth: Therapsids dominate; Capitanian extinction at the end.

Lopingian.earth: Siberian Traps erupt, causing the Great Dying.

Early Triassic.earth: Hothouse after the extinction; Lystrosaurus dominated land.

Late Triassic.earth: Carnian Pluvial Event; first dinosaurs and mammals appear.

Early Jurassic.earth: Atlantic begins opening; warm humid climate.

Middle Jurassic.earth: Sauropods diversify; Gondwana and Laurasia separate.

Early Cretaceous.earth: Gondwana breaks up; flowering plants appear.

Late Cretaceous.earth: High seas; Western Interior Seaway; Chicxulub impact.

Paleocene.earth: Warm, forested world recovering from the K–Pg extinction.

Eocene.earth: Warmest epoch of the Cenozoic; palm trees near the poles.

Oligocene.earth: Antarctica ices over; grasslands begin to spread.

Miocene.earth: Warm then cooling climate; kelp forests and grasslands expand.

Pliocene.earth: Isthmus of Panama forms; climate cools toward the ice ages.

Formation of Earth.title: Formation of Earth
Formation of Earth.desc: The Solar System condenses from a collapsing cloud of gas and dust; Earth accretes within a few tens of millions of years.

Moon-forming impact.title: Moon-forming impact
Moon-forming impact.desc: A Mars-sized planet, Theia, collides with the proto-Earth. The debris forms the Moon.

First oceans.title: First oceans
First oceans.desc: The oldest zircon crystals show that liquid water and continental crust already existed.

Last universal common ancestor.title: Last universal common ancestor
Last universal common ancestor.desc: LUCA, the ancestor of all living cells, lived around this time according to molecular-clock estimates.

Earliest evidence of life.title: Earliest evidence of life
Earliest evidence of life.desc: Carbon isotopes and possible stromatolites in Greenland rocks record early microbial life.

Microbial mats & stromatolites.title: Microbial mats & stromatolites
Microbial mats & stromatolites.desc: Well-preserved stromatolites in Western Australia show thriving microbial communities.

Oxygenic photosynthesis.title: Oxygenic photosynthesis
Oxygenic photosynthesis.desc: Cyanobacteria begin splitting water and releasing oxygen as a by-product.

Great Oxidation Event.title: Great Oxidation Event
Great Oxidation Event.desc: Free oxygen accumulates in the atmosphere for the first time, transforming the planet's chemistry.

Huronian glaciation.title: Huronian glaciation
Huronian glaciation.desc: The first great ice age, possibly triggered by oxygen destroying the methane greenhouse.

First complex cells?.title: First complex cells?
First complex cells?.desc: Grypania, a coiled macroscopic fossil, may be an early eukaryotic alga.

Eukaryotes.title: Eukaryotes
Eukaryotes.desc: Cells with nuclei and mitochondria — the ancestors of all plants, animals and fungi — are firmly established.

Sexual reproduction & multicellularity.title: Sexual reproduction & multicellularity
Sexual reproduction & multicellularity.desc: Bangiomorpha, a red alga, is the oldest known sexually reproducing, multicellular organism.

First fungi.title: First fungi
First fungi.desc: Microfossils such as Ourasphaira suggest fungi were present by the late Proterozoic.

Snowball Earth.title: Snowball Earth
Snowball Earth.desc: The Sturtian and Marinoan glaciations may have frozen the entire planet.

First animals.title: First animals
First animals.desc: Sponge biomarkers hint at the earliest animals; animals would soon diversify in the Ediacaran.

Ediacaran biota.title: Ediacaran biota
Ediacaran biota.desc: The first large complex multicellular organisms, such as Dickinsonia and Charnia, live on the sea floor.

Cambrian explosion.title: Cambrian explosion
Cambrian explosion.desc: Most major animal groups appear rapidly in the fossil record, with eyes, shells and legs.

First trilobites.title: First trilobites
First trilobites.desc: Trilobites, iconic armoured arthropods, appear and will dominate the seas for 270 million years.

First vertebrates.title: First vertebrates
First vertebrates.desc: Small jawless fish like Haikouichthys swim in Cambrian seas.

Plants colonise land.title: Plants colonise land
Plants colonise land.desc: Spores of the earliest land plants, related to liverworts, appear in the fossil record.

Late Ordovician extinction.title: Late Ordovician extinction
Late Ordovician extinction.desc: Glaciation and falling sea levels kill ~85% of marine species.

First jawed fish.title: First jawed fish
First jawed fish.desc: Jaws evolve from gill arches; jawed vertebrates quickly diversify.

First vascular plants.title: First vascular plants
First vascular plants.desc: Cooksonia, a tiny plant with water-conducting tissues, grows in damp ground.

First land animal.title: First land animal
First land animal.desc: Pneumodesmus, a millipede, is the oldest known animal to breathe air on land.

First insects.title: First insects
First insects.desc: Rhyniognatha from the Rhynie chert is among the oldest known insects.

First forests.title: First forests
First forests.desc: Tree-like plants such as Wattieza and Archaeopteris form the first forests.

Fish walk toward land.title: Fish walk toward land
Fish walk toward land.desc: Tiktaalik, a lobe-finned fish with a neck and wrist bones, bridges fish and tetrapods.

Late Devonian extinction.title: Late Devonian extinction
Late Devonian extinction.desc: A series of extinction pulses wipes out ~70% of species, especially reef builders.

First tetrapods.title: First tetrapods
First tetrapods.desc: Four-limbed vertebrates like Acanthostega and Ichthyostega live in swamps.

First seed plants.title: First seed plants
First seed plants.desc: Seeds free plants from dependence on water for reproduction.

First flying animals.title: First flying animals
First flying animals.desc: Winged insects (Pterygota) take to the air, the first animals to fly.

First amniotes.title: First amniotes
First amniotes.desc: Hard-shelled eggs let vertebrates reproduce away from water; Hylonomus is an early reptile.

First synapsids.title: First synapsids
First synapsids.desc: The lineage leading to mammals splits from reptiles.

Carboniferous rainforest collapse.title: Carboniferous rainforest collapse
Carboniferous rainforest collapse.desc: Coal forests fragment as the climate dries, reshaping land life.

The Great Dying.title: The Great Dying
The Great Dying.desc: The Permian–Triassic extinction kills ~90% of marine and ~70% of land species.

First dinosaurs.title: First dinosaurs
First dinosaurs.desc: Early dinosaurs like Eoraptor and Herrerasaurus appear in South America.

First flying vertebrates.title: First flying vertebrates
First flying vertebrates.desc: Pterosaurs become the first vertebrates capable of powered flight.

First mammals.title: First mammals
First mammals.desc: Small, shrew-like mammaliaforms such as Adelobasileus appear.

Triassic–Jurassic extinction.title: Triassic–Jurassic extinction
Triassic–Jurassic extinction.desc: Volcanism as Pangaea rifts kills many archosaurs, opening the way for dinosaurs.

Pangaea breaks up.title: Pangaea breaks up
Pangaea breaks up.desc: The supercontinent splits into Laurasia and Gondwana as the Atlantic opens.

First birds.title: First birds
First birds.desc: Archaeopteryx, a feathered dinosaur, links dinosaurs and birds.

First flowering plants.title: First flowering plants
First flowering plants.desc: Angiosperms appear and soon transform terrestrial ecosystems.

First bees.title: First bees
First bees.desc: Bees evolve alongside flowering plants; pollination partnerships begin.

End of the dinosaurs.title: End of the dinosaurs
End of the dinosaurs.desc: An asteroid strikes Chicxulub; ~75% of species, including all non-avian dinosaurs, go extinct.

Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum.title: Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum
Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum.desc: A rapid carbon release warms Earth by 5–8 °C; modern mammal orders spread.

Whales return to the sea.title: Whales return to the sea
Whales return to the sea.desc: Pakicetus, a land-dwelling ancestor of whales, lives in what is now Pakistan.

Antarctica freezes.title: Antarctica freezes
Antarctica freezes.desc: The Antarctic ice sheet forms as Earth cools at the Eocene–Oligocene transition.

First apes.title: First apes
First apes.desc: Apes (Hominoidea) split from Old World monkeys.

Human lineage splits from chimps.title: Human lineage splits from chimps
Human lineage splits from chimps.desc: Sahelanthropus may be one of the earliest members of the human lineage.

Lucy.title: Lucy
Lucy.desc: Australopithecus afarensis walks upright on two legs in East Africa.

Genus Homo.title: Genus Homo
Genus Homo.desc: The first members of our genus appear; stone tools soon follow.

Ice ages begin.title: Ice ages begin
Ice ages begin.desc: Quaternary glaciation: ice sheets advance and retreat in ~100,000-year cycles.

Homo sapiens.title: Homo sapiens
Homo sapiens.desc: Anatomically modern humans appear in Africa.

Agriculture.title: Agriculture
Agriculture.desc: The Neolithic Revolution: humans domesticate plants and animals.
